mechanism.description: Long-term accumulation of Advanced Glycation End-products (AGEs) in the arterial wall creates stiff, non-compliant vessels that do not benefit from late-stage glycemic control.
Chronic diabetes leads to cardiac autonomic neuropathy (CAN), which increases the duration of the QTc interval and heightens the risk of fatal ventricular arrhythmias during nocturnal hypoglycemia.

Disease progression leads to near-total beta-cell loss, making patients entirely dependent on exogenous insulin, which has a higher risk of producing 'brittle' glycemic swings compared to newly diagnosed patients.
Prior ischemic damage provides an arrhythmogenic substrate (scar tissue) that is susceptible to catecholamine-induced sudden cardiac death during hypoglycemic episodes.
Patients with prior events frequently take beta-blockers, which mask the tremors and palpitations of hypoglycemia, leading to delayed glucose rescue.
Fixed atherosclerotic stenoses in coronary and cerebral arteries make these territories highly vulnerable to transient supply-demand mismatch during glycemic fluctuations.
Reduced eGFR significantly prolongs the half-life of insulin and secretagogues, making intensive-arm patients prone to prolonged and difficult-to-treat hypoglycemia.

Because the Outcome Alignment gate (major CV outcomes/mortality) fails, the abstract is irrelevant to the specified mechanism.
abstracts_analyzed.evidence_quote: Compared to the standard arm, eGFR was lower by 2.9 and 3.3mL/min/1.73m2 in the intensive arm at year 1 and year 4.
abstracts_analyzed.title: Effects of Intensive Blood Pressure Lowering on Kidney Tubule Injury in CKD: A Longitudinal Subgroup Analysis in SPRINT.
